issues.issue: The flat prohibition on any disclosure of the Memorandum without prior written consent sits against c011 (Confidential/Trade Secret), which expressly permits distribution to the recipient's own financial and legal advisors. A court would have to decide which permission governs a disclosure to advisors.

Transfer is permitted only "as provided in the Note Purchase Agreement", while c125 states specific exceptions (family trusts, wholly-owned affiliates, operation of law) and c017 says transfers are only in the Manager's discretion. The three statements of the transfer rule are not identical.

The undertaking to provide additional information reaches only what the Company can obtain "WITHOUT UNREASONABLE EFFORT OR EXPENSE", a boundary the provision does not fix. What counts as unreasonable is left entirely at large.

The reserved right of the Manager and its affiliates to modify "ANY OF THE TERMS OF THE OFFERING AND THE OFFERING DOCUMENTS" before the final closing cannot be squared with c132, which makes any modification of the Note Purchase Agreement, the Notes or the Security Agreement ineffective without a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. Investors who closed early would be affected by unilateral changes the amendment clause forbids.

"AT ANY TIME BEFORE A CLOSING" does not say which closing: on one reading the offering may be terminated only before the initial closing, on another before any later closing. The article "a" carries the whole termination right.

The permission to share the Memorandum with the recipient's own financial and legal advisors is inconsistent with c001, which prohibits any disclosure of the contents without the Manager's prior written consent. The two consent regimes coexist in the same front matter.

The flat statement that "The Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company" cannot be reconciled with c019 and c126, which allow Company Borrowings to take security in the same Collateral senior in priority to the Noteholders. A Noteholder could read the summary as a first-priority promise.

The stated formation purpose is lending the capital raised by the sale of Notes, whereas c019 and c080 permit Note proceeds to be used for expenses, compensation and a reserve fund. The scope of permitted use of subscription proceeds is stated twice, differently.

Closings are expected monthly "through May 1, 2009", while c113 (Closing) fixes the final closing at the last day of the sixth full quarter after the Initial Closing, estimated June 30, 2009. The two statements of the closing window do not match.

"[S]ubject to a minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized" does not say over what period the average is struck, so a quarter below 8% may or may not breach it. The word "average" is doing all the work and is unanchored.

This describes the rate protection as a "minimum average rate", whereas c093 (Note Terms — Interest) states the Floating Rate "will not be less than 8% on an annualized basis for a calendar year" — a floor, not an average. The two formulations promise different things.

This says a Noteholder "may not request prepayment" until the Note has been held a year, while c107 permits a request at any time provided the prepayment date is no earlier than the anniversary and adds sixty days' notice and a quarter-end condition. The two statements of the prepayment mechanic differ.

The unqualified statement that Noteholders "will be secured creditors" is hard to square with c126, which permits a Company Borrowing to hold a senior security interest in the same Collateral, and with c201's warning that the security may not be perfected in seniority. The quality of the creditor status is stated differently in different places.

The permission for borrowings secured by liens senior to the Notes contradicts the unqualified security promise in c012 and c098. A court asked whether Noteholders bargained for first-priority collateral would have to choose between them.

The promise that the Company "will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market" cannot be reconciled with c068 (Credit Evaluations), which expressly contemplates loans to borrowers already in default on other obligations or without income sufficient to qualify at a bank. Those are the defining features of sub-prime lending.

The claim of a "proven lending record" with no investor loss of principal sits against c022 and c198, which state the Company has no operating history and that past performance cannot be relied on. The two passages point in different directions on what the investor may rely on.

"The Servicer will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company" conflicts with c047, which lets the Manager retain other firms "in lieu of the Servicer", and with c076, which allows purchases from unrelated third parties. "All" cannot stand alongside those permissions.

The Manager's reserved right to terminate all of its business relationship with the Company "at any time" contradicts c127 (Restricted Actions), which forbids the Manager to withdraw as sole manager without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. Read together, the Manager both may and may not walk away unilaterally.

"10% of late charges on delinquent Portfolio Loan payments received by the Company" leaves it unclear whether "received by the Company" qualifies the late charges or the payments, and so what the 10% is measured on. The modifier can attach to either noun.

The fee is only "[a]nticipated to average between three percent (3%) and six percent (6%)", which states an expectation rather than any binding limit on what the Servicer may charge. Nothing in the provision caps the actual commission.

This states documentation and processing fees are "anticipated to average approximately $1,000 per loan", while c119 states the same fees are anticipated to aggregate "approximately $1,000 -$2,000 per Portfolio Loan". The two disclosures of the same charge give different figures.

"Manager Expenses" is defined as everything "other than those borne by the Company or Servicer", which is circular: each of the three expense definitions is stated by exclusion of the others. The residual category has no independent content.

This states the Company bears its organizational fees and costs without limit, whereas c116 states the same obligation capped at the greater of $500,000 or 1% of aggregate Principal of outstanding Notes. The same defined term "Company Expenses" is given two different contents.

The provision opens by stating that a Delaware manager is accountable to members as a fiduciary and closes by stating the Manager has no fiduciary obligation to the Company's members either. The two propositions in the same paragraph pull against each other.

The exculpation standard here is "fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct", while c133 (Exculpation and Indemnification) uses "willful misconduct or gross negligence" for the same protection. Gross negligence is excepted in one place and not the other.

The indemnity carve-out is "fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct", whereas c133 describes the same Company indemnity as unavailable for "willful misconduct or gross negligence". A grossly negligent but honest Manager is indemnified under one and not the other.
Noteholders are told to "rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager", a standard the Memorandum never defines or makes enforceable. Whether this creates any obligation at all is contestable.

The parenthetical cross-reference "(See 'Fiduciary Responsibility of the Managing Member.')" points to no such heading; the corresponding section, c038, is headed NO FIDUCIARY RESPONSIBILITY OF MANAGER TO NOTEHOLDERS and says the opposite. The signpost and the text it points to disagree.

The Company will "generally" charge "the rate generally prevailing in the geographical areas where the security property is located for loans to comparable borrowers of similar size, duration and security" — a benchmark with no source and two hedges. Nothing fixes the rate the Company must charge.

The Manager's right to retain other firms "in lieu of the Servicer" is inconsistent with c026's statement that "[t]he Servicer will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company". One provision makes the Servicer exclusive and the other displaceable.

The definition of "Related Party Loans" turns on borrowers "affiliated with" the Manager, Members or Servicer or owned by "their family members", neither of which is defined or bounded. Whether a given borrower falls inside the 20% cap depends on that undefined reach.

This caps Related Party Loans at 20% of total Company assets "at any time", while c075 restates the same cap as measured only "upon the closing of the Related Party Loan in question". A continuous covenant and a closing-date test are materially different obligations.

Related Party Loan terms must be "consistent with the lending standards and policies set forth above" and with terms "typically offered" to unaffiliated borrowers, neither of which supplies a measurable benchmark. "Typically" leaves the comparison at large.

The buy-back is triggered only by "any material event of default", and no materiality threshold is supplied anywhere in the Memorandum. Whether a given default triggers the Manager's purchase obligation turns on that undefined word.

c075 restates this same obligation without the materiality qualifier — the loan "must be purchased ... if the Loan is in default more than 90 days". The trigger for the Manager's purchase obligation is stated twice, differently.

Allocation of loan opportunities is left to the Manager "after consideration of all relevant factors, including" a non-exhaustive list, so the enumerated factors constrain nothing. The catch-all swallows the specifics.

The Manager and Principals will devote "only so much time to the business of the Company as is reasonably required", a commitment with no measurable content. What is reasonably required is exactly what would be in dispute.

The Manager's "first priority will usually be" to recover the Company's full invested capital — "usually" converts a duty into a description of habit. Nothing in the sentence binds the Manager in any particular sale.

The purchase price must be "not less than any of the following: (i) ... (ii) ... or (iii)", which can mean not less than the highest of the three or merely not less than one of them. The word "any", coupled with "or", makes the affiliate-sale price floor genuinely two-way.

The provision applies criteria to "Sponsored Investment Funds or Private Clients", terms defined nowhere in the Memorandum, which elsewhere defines only "Other Sponsored Investment Funds" (c052). Which entities are caught cannot be determined from the instrument.

Lending is limited to real estate "located primarily in the United States, its territories and possessions", and "primarily" fixes no percentage or test. The one geographic constraint on the portfolio is expressed by an unquantified adverb.

The bare table gives loan-to-value ratios only for "Improved Property" and "Land", with no rule for a construction or partly improved property, which c061 expressly contemplates. Which of the two lines applies to such a loan is not stated.

These are announced as a "strict set of guidelines", yet c065 says the ratios "generally will not exceed" the stated percentages and c066 disapplies them entirely for purchase-money and refinancing transactions. "Strict" cannot be reconciled with those qualifications.
The 20% limit is measured against the "Company's entire Loan Portfolio", a term the Memorandum never defines, and no measuring date is given. The limit cannot be applied without supplying both.

The provision limits lending "primarily" to U.S. Properties but allows up to 20% of "total Company Capital" in non-U.S. loans; neither "primarily" nor "total Company Capital" is defined. The cap and the qualifier are measured on different, unstated bases.

The express 20% non-U.S. allowance sits against c013, which describes the lending purpose as financing real estate "throughout the United States". One says U.S. only, the other permits a fifth abroad.

The loan-to-value test is applied to a valuation "as determined by either the Manager or an independent written appraisal", so the Manager may itself supply the value against which its own compliance is judged. The word "generally" further loosens the limit.

The Manager may accept "any reasonable financing terms that it deems to be in the best interests of the Company, in its sole discretion", combining an objective standard with a wholly subjective one. Whether reasonableness is reviewable at all is left open.

Deeming affiliate purchase-money financing not to be a Related Party Loan removes it from the 20% cap in c049 and the default buy-back in c051, which are the Memorandum's stated protections against affiliate lending. The exception undercuts the rule.

Portfolio Loans of up to six years made late in the offering period (c113 allows a final closing in mid-2009) would mature after the Notes' 31 December 2014 Maturity Date in c092 and outlast the Company term in c124. The lending term and the repayment term do not fit together.

Expressly permitting loans to borrowers already in default on other obligations or without income sufficient to qualify at a bank cannot be reconciled with c020's promise that the Company "will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market". The lending policy and the marketing statement point in opposite directions.
The parenthetical directs the reader to "VII. Risk Factors ~ Uninsured Losses", but the Risk Factors section contains no such heading. The cross-reference has no referent in the instrument.

This appears as escrow condition (c) under c069's instruction that the escrow agent "not ... disburse any funds until the following conditions are met", yet it states only that the Manager does not intend to arrange mortgage insurance. As drafted it cannot operate as a condition at all.

The expectation that "all Company loans" will be serviced by the Servicer sits against c047, which permits the Manager to retain other firms in lieu of the Servicer for loan servicing. The exclusivity is asserted in one place and denied in another.

This measures the 20% Related Party Loan cap only "upon the closing of the Related Party Loan in question", while c049 imposes it "at any time" on a continuing basis. Whether later growth in related-party exposure breaches the cap depends on which version governs.

"Generally, the purchase price ... will not exceed the par value of the note or its fair market value, whichever is lower" is immediately qualified by a premium exception resting on the Manager's own belief. Between "generally" and the exception, no enforceable price limit remains.

The clause "to achieve comparable with Sponsored Investment Funds" is missing a word and cannot be read as written, leaving the scope of permitted co-lending transactions uncertain. The sentence's object is simply absent.

The diversification limit bites only "[a]fter the second year of the Company's term" and is measured against "the capital of the Company", neither of which the Memorandum defines with a start date or a formula. Both the trigger and the denominator are unfixed.

This permits sales of non-performing loans and foreclosed property to the Servicer or affiliates without repeating the minimum-price protections that c059 imposes on exactly such affiliate sales. Whether the c059 floor applies to these sales is left open.

The qualified statement that the Company "does not presently intend" to resell and "may occasionally sell" loans cannot be squared with c020's flat statement that the Company "will not source loans for the purpose of resale". One is a covenant, the other a present intention.
The closing cross-reference is to "Risks and Other Important Factors - Risks of Leverage", a heading that does not exist in the Memorandum's Risk Factors section. The pointer leads nowhere.

Subscriptions are accepted "in the discretion of the Managing Member", a term the Memorandum never defines; acceptance is elsewhere vested in the Manager. Who may accept a subscription cannot be answered from the words used.

The stated purpose extends to "such other directly related activities ... as the Manager deems reasonably necessary or appropriate", an open catch-all sitting against the enumerated lending and foreclosure activities. Its reach is set by the Manager's own view.

"The Company may admit additional or substitute managers" is difficult to reconcile with c127, which bars the Manager from withdrawing as sole manager without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. Substitution and prohibited withdrawal overlap.

Defining "Servicer" as one or more delegate entities collectively is in tension with c026's statement that the Servicer (Bar-K) "will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company". The identity and exclusivity of the Servicer differ between the two.

"A minimum investment is 20,000 Units, in the discretion of the Manager" does not say whether the minimum itself is waivable at the Manager's discretion or whether the discretion relates only to fractional Units. The sentence supports either reading.
Subscription acceptance is vested in "the Manager, in its sole discretion" here, but in "the Managing Member" in c084. The two provisions name different decision-makers for the same act.

The defined term "(the 'Maturity Date')" is appended to the extension clause, leaving it unclear whether the Maturity Date is 31 December 2014 or the extended date up to six months later. The definition attaches equally to either.

c096 separately defines "Maturity Date" as the last day of the Note's term, so the same term is defined twice in adjacent bullets. Which definition governs c124's two-year post-maturity term is then open.

"The Floating Rate will not be less than 8% on an annualized basis for a calendar year" can mean a floor on each quarterly rate or only that the year's rates must average 8%. The rate protection is the core economic term and the words support both readings.

c016 states the same protection as a "minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized", which is an average rather than a floor. The Executive Summary and the Summary of Principal Terms promise different things.

This defines "Maturity Date" as the last day of the Note's term, whereas c092 has already attached that defined term to the December 31, 2014 date subject to a six-month extension. The instrument carries two definitions of the same term.

The promise that repayment "shall be secured by an interest in the assets of the Company" is qualified elsewhere by c126, which lets a Company Borrowing take a senior interest in the same Collateral. The priority of the Noteholders' security is stated unqualified here and subordinated there.

The bar on accepting additional subscriptions "for any closing after the final closing" sits against c102, which lets the Manager solicit voluntary purchases of additional Units "from time to time" without any end date. Whether additional Units may be sold after the final closing is left unresolved.

The Manager's open-ended right to solicit additional Unit purchases "from time to time" is not squared with c100, which bars acceptance of additional subscriptions for any closing after the final closing. The two provisions set different end points for additional sales.

The Closing Account is held "for the exclusive purpose of holding subscription deposits" yet the Company may retain any interest earned "in consideration of its costs", which are neither identified nor capped. Exclusivity and retention of earnings sit awkwardly in one sentence.

The label "Minimum Holding Period" is attached to a permitted prepayment date rather than to any holding obligation, and every condition is waivable by the Company. What the defined term actually restricts is unclear on the face of the sentence.

c017 states the Noteholder "may not request prepayment" until it has held the Note a year, whereas this provision permits the request and restricts only the prepayment date, adding sixty days' notice and a quarter-end requirement. The two prepayment mechanics differ.

The Collateral Agent must act "on terms required by the Manager ... but only to the extent that such terms or actions are not prohibited under the Noteholder Agreements", while the same agreements are what set its powers. The limitation is circular and gives no workable boundary on subordination consents.

Acceleration on bankruptcy or dissolution is disapplied "to the extent the Company's obligations ... have been assumed by an affiliate of or successor in interest to the Company", with no standard for the assuming party's creditworthiness or the form of assumption. The exception can swallow the acceleration right.

Admission of members requires "the requisite approval of members", but c038 and this same provision state the Manager is the sole member, so the approval requirement is self-referential. It gives Noteholders no protection it appears to promise.

The final closing deadline here (last day of the sixth full quarter after the Initial Closing, estimated June 30, 2009) does not match c015, which says closings are expected monthly "through May 1, 2009". The offering period is stated twice with different end dates.

The organizational-cost cap is "a maximum of $500,000 or 1% of aggregate Principal of outstanding Notes, whichever amount is greater", with no date for measuring outstanding Principal. The ceiling floats with an unfixed denominator.
c036 states the same Company Expenses obligation with no cap at all on organizational fees and costs. The same defined term is given two different scopes in the same document.

Loan process and documentation fees are put at "approximately $1,000 -$2,000 per Portfolio Loan", while c034 states the same fees are anticipated to average approximately $1,000 per loan. The disclosure of the same charge differs between the two sections.

The requirement that borrower fees paid to the Company or Manager "shall be paid to Servicer" conflicts with c122, which permits the Manager, Members and their affiliates to be paid and retain origination, brokerage and other fees by Portfolio Borrowers. The same borrower-paid fees are both turned over and retained.

The permission to take borrower fees is "subject to restrictions with respect to Affiliated Transactions", a capitalized term that appears nowhere else and is nowhere defined. The only limit on this affiliate compensation right cannot be located.

The provision says the Company is restricted "in the amount of compensation it may receive", but everywhere else in the Memorandum the compensation restrictions govern what the Company pays to the Manager and Servicer. As written the restriction points the wrong way.

"The Company's initial term will terminate at the Manager's election upon the first to occur of" two dated events leaves it unclear whether termination is automatic on the earlier event or requires an election the Manager may withhold. The two mechanisms are combined in one sentence.

Transfers are barred "except for certain transfers to family trusts, to wholly-owned affiliates or by operation of law", and "certain" is never specified. Which transfers within those three categories are permitted is not stated.

This authorises a senior security interest in the Collateral for a Company Borrowing on terms set by the Manager, while c127 forbids the Company to create or permit any Lien on the Collateral without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. The senior-lien power and the consent right cannot both operate in full.

The consent right covers the enumerated acts "among other restrictions", so the list of protected matters is expressly non-exhaustive with no indication of what else is caught. The general phrase and the specific list pull against each other.

Beyond tax information, Noteholders receive only such reports and financial statements "as the Manager, in its discretion, may determine", so the reporting obligation has no fixed content. Whether any financial statement is owed at all is left to the obligor.

The sentence omits the words that would connect clauses (i) and (ii) to the amendment ("if such amendment ..."), so as written it says the Company Agreement may never be amended without Noteholder approval — or only in two unstated cases. It also conditions approval on the "Investor Documents", a term used nowhere else in the Memorandum.

The Majority in Interest requirement for modifications cannot be squared with c009, in which the Manager and its affiliates reserve the right to modify any of the terms of the Offering Documents before the final closing. One requires collective approval, the other reserves unilateral change.

The indemnity is denied only for "willful misconduct or gross negligence", whereas c041 states the same Company indemnity is unavailable for "fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct". Fraud and bad faith are excepted in one formulation and gross negligence in the other.

The power of attorney is granted by the Note Purchase Agreement yet covers documents "that the Members have expressly agreed to execute", although Noteholders are expressly not Members (c111). The class of documents the Manager may execute for a Noteholder is therefore empty or misdescribed.

The passage defines and uses "Comparable Yield" but then refers to the IRS requiring "a higher or lower Comparative Yield", a different term. The switch leaves the defined concept and the operative one out of alignment.

The provision abbreviates "unrelated business taxable income" as "(UBT)" while every later passage uses UBTI, so the defined abbreviation never reappears. The mismatch is a drafting slip in the only definition of the term.

The passage first states that on equity recharacterization amounts received "would not be treated as UBTI" and then states that income on loans funded by Company Borrowings "would constitute" debt-financed property generating UBTI. The two sentences cannot both be true as written.

The provision speaks of structuring the ownership so as not to subject "the Fund" to the Investment Company Act, using a term the Memorandum never defines (the issuer is the "Company"). It then adds an inconsistent "[i]n the alternative" reliance on a statutory exemption.

The warning that rates payable to Noteholders "may exceed" the California 10% usury threshold sits against c093's guaranteed 8% floor with an unlimited discretionary upside. Whether the Company could lawfully set the Floating Rate above the usury cap is left unaddressed.
The compliance undertaking is only to "use commercially reasonable efforts" in reliance on advisors, a standard the Memorandum nowhere measures. The undertaking's content is entirely in the adverb.

The statement that purchase of the Notes "will involve a high degree of risk" is difficult to square with c012's description of the offering as achieving "superior returns with a conservative risk profile". The summary and the risk section characterise the same investment oppositely.

The provision refers to "the inability of the Portfolio Manager to repay such Loan", though the party obliged to repay a Portfolio Loan is the Portfolio Borrower and no "Portfolio Manager" is defined. The mistaken term changes who the sentence is about.

The statement that the Company only "intends to require" adequate borrower insurance is weaker than c070, which makes satisfactory fire and casualty insurance naming the Company as loss payee a condition to any escrow disbursement. The insurance requirement is mandatory in one place and aspirational in the other.

The Manager and its members are said to receive "Company gains and certain other income" proportionally greater than Noteholder Interest, without identifying what those gains are or how they are measured. The phrase "certain other income" is unbounded.

The heading and text describe the Notes as carrying risks "typical of investments in private equity funds", though c018 and c130 make Noteholders creditors with no equity or profit interest. The characterisation of the instrument differs from the operative terms.

The statement that the Company has no operating history and that past performance cannot be relied on sits against c021's claim of a "proven lending record" with no investor loss of principal. The two passages give opposite guidance on reliance.

The warning that there is "no assurance that the Noteholders' security interest will be perfected in seniority" cannot be squared with the unqualified security statements in c012 and c018 that the Notes are secured by the Company's assets and Noteholders are secured creditors. One disclaims what the other promises.

This defines the Investment Company Act of 1940 as "the Company Act", although c003 and c160 have already defined the same statute as the "Investment Company Act", and c213 calls it the "Companies Act". The same statute carries three defined labels in one instrument.

The trust category is limited to an "IRREVOCABLE TRUST", a narrower class than Rule 501 itself uses, so a qualifying trust may fail the representation it is asked to make. The single adjective controls eligibility.

c216 extends qualification to "a living trust or other revocable trust" whose grantors and trustees qualify, which is inconsistent with limiting trusts to irrevocable ones here. Whether a revocable trust may subscribe depends on which clause governs.

The clause refers to an investment company "registered under the United States Companies Act of 1940" and defines that as the "Companies Act", misnaming the Investment Company Act of 1940 referred to elsewhere. The mistake goes to the identification of a qualifying investor class.

This qualifies entities "not formed for the purpose of acquiring the Note", while c217 provides separate criteria for entities that were formed for that purpose. Which representation such an entity must make is not settled between them.
The clause qualifies an entity whose equity owners qualify under clauses (i)–(v) "or this clause (vi)", which is circular self-reference. Applied literally the look-through never terminates.

This says the Summary of Principal Terms is qualified in its entirety by the Note Purchase Agreement alone, while c009 qualifies the Memorandum by all of the Offering Documents and c084 qualifies only Sections III, IV and V. The three qualification clauses do not describe the same hierarchy.
